newsitem.title: USA: Ceridian settles age bias case for $28.5 million.
newsitem.headline: Ceridian settles age bias case for $28.5 million.

text.p: An age discrimination suit brought by employees of the former Control Data Corp. was settled for $28.5 million Wednesday as the case was about to go to trial.
Nancy Foltz, a spokeswoman for Ceridian Corp., one of Control Data's successor companies, said Ceridian would pay $24 million, while Control Data Systems, the other successor, would pay $4.5 million.
The money will go to 313 people who were laid off by Control Data Corp. The company was restructured in 1992.
Ceridian's stock gained $1.625 to $40.50 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange after the settlement was announced.
Suits filed by the employees were consolidated in 1995 into a single suit to determine if a "pattern or practice" of age discrimination occurred during the layoffs.

A jury had been empaneled in federal court and the trial to determine the "pattern or practice" issue was about to begin when the settlement was reached. Had the companies been found guilty in the trial, which was to start Wednesday, the former employees could have sued later for damages.
During the late 1980s, the company lost in excess of $1 billion, and its work force fell from 60,000 in 1983 to 10,000 in 1990, after divestitures and voluntary and involuntary terminations.
At one time, more than 1,000 laid-off workers were involved in the suits, but settlements and decisions reduced that number.
Ceridian had denied the charges, saying age had no bearing on the downsizing decisions Control Data made in the 1980s.

Ceridian provides systems and services for human resources departments and financial transaction services for trucking and gambling companies. The company also provides consumer and retail data to the electronic media through its Arbitron division.
The company reported 1996 earnings of $181.9 million on revenues of $1.5 billion.
Control Data Systems provides integration of computer systems to businesses and government.
Judge John Tunheim of the U.S. District Court dismissed the suit after the settlement was announced.
